entry.title: Merge pull request #61 from Harsh-Upadhayay/fix/import-media-local-an…
entry.content:
Merge pull request #61 from Harsh-Upadhayay/fix/import-media-local-and-ci-sse

fix(anki): persist imported media locally; stop spurious seed prompt; fix SSE race

entry.title: fix(anki): persist imported media locally; stop spurious seed prompt;…
entry.content:
fix(anki): persist imported media locally; stop spurious seed prompt; fix SSE race

Three related bugs from the client-side-parse / P2P work.

1. Source device showed no media after a client-side import. The parse
   worker built the manifest but never saved the decoded blobs to the
   local anki_media store, and with P2P-primary the media wasn't
   uploaded to the server either -- so the importing device's own cards
   resolved nothing (local miss -> /api/media/{hash} 404). The worker
   now persists each blob as it's decoded, pinned: written with no
   LRU-meta entry, and enforceMediaCacheLimit only evicts hashes that
   have meta, so a deck you imported here keeps its media offline
   forever with no cloud upload and no dependency on a peer.

   Media received over P2P (ReceiveTransferBanner, SeedMediaPanel) is
   pinned the same way via a new saveMediaBlobPinned, since pure-P2P
   media may exist nowhere else -- previously it went through the
   LRU-capped saveMediaBlob and could be evicted and lost. Media lazily
   fetched per-card from the server keeps using saveMediaBlob (LRU):
   it's server-backed, so evict-and-refetch is fine.

2. The "Get your media" seed panel fired for essentially every deck,
   new or existing. Its trigger was "any manifest hash missing from the
   local cache" -- but with lazy fetch + a 50 MB LRU, missing-locally is
   the normal resting state. It now fires only for media missing locally
   AND absent from the server (bulk /api/media/check): i.e. genuinely
   nowhere-reachable, the real pure-P2P-seeding case. Anything the
   server has just lazy-fetches per card.

3. CI Backend failure: TestSyncEventsStreamsPublishedEvents, context
   deadline exceeded. The SSE handler flushed its ": connected" greeting
   before subscribing to the hub, so a client pushing the instant it saw
   the greeting could have its poke published before the handler was
   listening (non-blocking Publish drops it). A real correctness gap,
   not just a test flake. Subscribe now happens before the greeting, so
   "greeting received" reliably means "subscribed."

Verified in real browsers against the Go backend: after a single-device
client import, the source's anki_media store holds the blobs and no seed
prompt appears on reload; the two-device P2P transfer still lands media
on the receiver; and the SSE test passes 20/20 locally.

Closes #60

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Merge pull request #59 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/p2p-seed-new-devices
entry.content:
Merge pull request #59 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/p2p-seed-new-devices

feat(p2p): seed a new device's media P2P-first from any online device

entry.title: feat(p2p): seed a new device's media P2P-first from any online device
entry.content:
feat(p2p): seed a new device's media P2P-first from any online device

Closes out the plan in docs/plans/2026-07-04-client-apkg-parse-p2p-media.md.
A fresh device (new install, or a reinstall) syncs the collection and
gets its mediaManifest, but starts with no cached media. The existing
per-card lazy fetch from the cloud store already covers this -- that
stays untouched as the permanent safety net -- but this adds a faster,
proactive path: request the missing media P2P from any of the user's
other devices that happen to be online, not just the one that
originally imported it.

- SeedMediaPanel: shown once (per mount) when a device detects media
  its own synced collection references but doesn't have locally.
  Creates a pull-mode signaling room and waits, bounded by the room's
  server-side TTL like MediaTransferPanel. No cloud-fallback state
  machine needed here -- if P2P never lands, cards just keep working
  via the existing lazy fetch, so this panel is a pure UX accelerator,
  not something the app depends on.
- SeedResponder: mounted app-wide, answers a pull room only if this
  device actually has local media to offer (getAllStoredMediaRefs()
  is non-empty). That "only if" matters: the device that originally
  imported a deck reads media straight from the ephemeral .apkg File
  during a P2P send and never persists its own copy (see
  MediaTransferPanel), so it would otherwise try to answer with an
  empty manifest. Skipping it routes seeding requests to whichever
  device actually received and durably cached media.
- getAllStoredMediaRefs() (anki-v3.ts): new export enumerating what's
  actually sitting in the anki_media IndexedDB store, since a
  device's local cache is a subset of its synced collection's full
  manifest (the 50MB LRU cap evicts entries).

Verified with a real three-browser-context E2E: A imports and P2P-sends
to B (matching PR7's flow, so B ends up with a durable local media
cache); a fresh third context C signs into the same account, syncs the
collection, and its SeedMediaPanel discovers B (not A, which has
nothing to offer) via SeedResponder and receives the media P2P --
confirmed via IndexedDB record counts on both sides. 2/2 clean runs.

Known limitation, called out rather than solved: no coordination if
two devices could both answer the same pull room. Acceptable for a
first cut.

Closes #58

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Merge pull request #57 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/p2p-transfer-ui
entry.content:
Merge pull request #57 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/p2p-transfer-ui

feat(p2p): make direct transfer the primary path for import media

entry.title: feat(p2p): make direct transfer the primary path for import media
entry.content:
feat(p2p): make direct transfer the primary path for import media

Wires the P2P engine (#54/#55) and signaling backend (#52/#53) into
the actual import flow. Direct device-to-device transfer is now the
primary way a deck's media reaches another device; the cloud store
stays available but only as a fallback when nobody answers.

- importAnkiPackage's client-parse path no longer auto-uploads to the
  cloud (uploadMedia now defaults to false in client.ts/worker.ts) --
  it returns an ImportOutcome with an optional pendingMediaTransfer
  the UI drives. Extracted the upload-missing-media logic worker.ts
  used to own into apkg/cloudMediaUpload.ts so both the worker and the
  new UI fallback path share one retry/batching implementation.

- MediaTransferPanel: shown on the importing device once parsing
  finds media to move. Announces a P2P room and waits -- no hard
  timeout on its own (bounded by the signaling room's 10-minute TTL) --
  with messaging that keeping both devices online is what makes this
  fast, plus an escape hatch to switch to cloud upload immediately and
  live transfer progress either way.

- ReceiveTransferBanner: rendered app-wide, polls for an open room
  from the user's own other devices (piggybacked on the existing
  sync-tick cadence, no new polling loop) and offers to receive.

Per the user's explicit call: a peer that never comes online should
wait for P2P with clear "why it's waiting" messaging rather than the
app silently uploading to the cloud as a parallel default -- cloud is
a genuine fallback, not a hedge that runs every time.

peer.ts's connect() now returns {promise, cancel} instead of a bare
promise, needed so the panel's "use cloud instead" button can abort a
still-waiting handshake. Building this surfaced a real bug caught only
by live-browser testing: canceling before any peer has answered closes
an RTCPeerConnection that's still in "new"/"checking" state, and Chrome
does not reliably fire connectionstatechange for that case -- the
promise would hang instead of rejecting. Fixed by racing a dedicated
cancellation promise alongside the connection-state listener rather
than depending on the event alone.

Verified end-to-end with two real signed-in browser sessions against
the actual UI and Go backend: importing a deck on device A showed the
transfer panel, device B's receive banner picked up the room and
accepted, and real media bytes landed in B's IndexedDB store (3/3
clean runs). Separately verified the cloud-fallback button: clicking
it immediately (before any peer joins) correctly cancels the P2P wait
and lands the same blobs in the server's content-addressed store.

Closes #56

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Merge pull request #55 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/p2p-transfer-client
entry.content:
Merge pull request #55 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/p2p-transfer-client

feat(p2p): direct media transfer over WebRTC

entry.title: feat(p2p): direct media transfer over WebRTC
entry.content:
feat(p2p): direct media transfer over WebRTC

Frontend transfer engine for direct device-to-device media (built on
the signaling mailbox from #52). Three modules, no third-party WebRTC
helper library:

- signaling.ts: thin REST client over /api/p2p/rooms*.
- peer.ts: an RTCPeerConnection wrapper. One connect() covers both the
  offering and answering roles rather than two near-duplicate
  functions, since the only real difference is who sends the offer vs
  the answer -- ICE trickling, mailbox polling, and waiting for the
  channel to open are identical either way.
- transfer.ts: the DataChannel wire protocol -- manifest -> want-list
  (diffed by the receiver against what it already has) -> chunked file
  send with bufferedAmount backpressure -> ack -> done. Sender and
  receiver are plain functions over a narrow DataChannelLike interface
  (send/addEventListener/bufferedAmount), which is what makes them unit
  testable against an in-memory mock channel pair instead of requiring
  real WebRTC for every test.

Not wired into any UI yet -- this is the transfer engine on its own,
verified two ways:

- Unit tests (mock channel pair): full transfer + correct bytes,
  skipping already-had files, resolving immediately when nothing is
  wanted, dropping a file that fails hash verification, and a
  regression test for the bug below.
- A real two-Chrome-tab E2E harness (bundled via esbuild, served
  alongside the actual Go backend) driving connect()/runSender/
  runReceiver with a genuine WebRTC handshake through the live
  signaling routes. This caught a real bug the mock couldn't: a data
  channel can report readyState "open" a moment before the underlying
  transport is symmetrically ready, occasionally dropping the very
  first message sent right after open (~50% of runs in testing).
  transfer.ts now retries the initial manifest send on an interval
  until the receiver's want-list arrives, which made 3/3 live-browser
  runs pass cleanly after the fix (previously ~50%).

Closes #54

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Merge pull request #53 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/p2p-signaling
entry.content:
Merge pull request #53 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/p2p-signaling

feat(p2p): signaling registry and routes for direct device transfer

entry.title: feat(p2p): signaling registry and routes for direct device transfer
entry.content:
feat(p2p): signaling registry and routes for direct device transfer

WebRTC needs a way for two devices to exchange an SDP offer/answer and
ICE candidates before they can open a direct peer connection between
themselves. This is that handshake mailbox and nothing more — the
server relays opaque JSON payloads and never joins the connection or
sees the media that eventually flows over it.

internal/signal: an in-memory Registry of throwaway rooms behind one
mutex (every operation is a quick map/slice touch, so an RWMutex would
add complexity without buying anything). Sequence numbers are assigned
under the same lock as the append that needs them, so two concurrent
posts can't race for the same number. Append/After both refresh a
room's expiry, so a slow ICE negotiation can't get reaped mid-handshake;
an idle room is swept by a ticker-driven janitor a fixed interval after
it goes quiet. Rooms carry a Mode (push: an importing device is
offering media; pull: a new device is requesting it) — both directions
share the exact same message protocol, so one Room type covers the
import-transfer and cross-device-seeding scenarios from the P2P plan.

internal/handlers/p2p.go wires five thin routes over it
(POST/GET /api/p2p/rooms, DELETE/POST/GET on
/api/p2p/rooms/{roomID}[/messages]), following the existing
decode-delegate-map-status pattern and the writeUploadError-style
sentinel-error mapping (ErrRoomNotFound -> 404).

Nothing consumes this yet on the frontend — that's the next PR. This
is backend-only groundwork, verified with live curl round-trips
(create, discover, post/read messages with own-echo exclusion, close,
post-to-closed-room 404) against a running server in addition to the
unit tests.

Closes #52

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Merge pull request #51 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/live-sync-sse
entry.content:
Merge pull request #51 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/live-sync-sse

feat(sync): live sync via SSE nudge, other devices update in ~1s

entry.title: feat(sync): live sync via SSE nudge, other devices update in ~1s
entry.content:
feat(sync): live sync via SSE nudge, other devices update in ~1s

Devices found out about each other's changes by polling /api/sync/pull
every 15s (App.tsx), so a review on one device could take up to ~15-30s
to appear on another that was already open. The merge logic in
internal/sync/sync.go stays the single source of truth on purpose —
porting it to the client would mean two implementations that drift, and
would reintroduce a "both devices online at once" requirement for what
is otherwise an async, offline-tolerant design (a device that's asleep
just catches up on its next connect).

So this only shortens notification latency, not the architecture:
device -> Go merge (unchanged) -> device, with the server nudging other
connected devices instead of them waiting on their own clock.

- internal/events: an in-memory Hub fans out content-free "state
  changed" pokes (origin device id + timestamp) to a user's connected
  devices. Mutex-guarded subscriber map; Publish never blocks (a full
  channel buffer just drops the poke — harmless, since the poll
  fallback and pull-on-reconnect both cover any gap).
- GET /api/sync/events (SSE, not WebSockets: plain HTTP, one-directional,
  EventSource reconnects on its own). SyncPush publishes one poke per
  successful merge, tagged with the pushing device's clientId (added to
  models.Meta) so that device can ignore its own echo.
- Client opens an EventSource on login and pulls immediately on a poke
  from another device. The 15s poll stays untouched as the fallback for
  old browsers or SSE-hostile proxies. The push side needed no changes:
  db.ts already debounces a push ~2.5s after a local mutation.

Verified end-to-end with two real browser sessions against the Go
backend: importing a deck on device A appeared on device B's already-open
Anki Decks tab in 505ms, versus up to 15s on the old poll-only path;
confirmed durable via a fresh reload reading the same state back out of
IndexedDB.

Closes #50

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Merge pull request #49 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/client-apkg-parse
entry.content:
Merge pull request #49 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/client-apkg-parse

feat(anki): parse .apkg in the browser, upload only missing media

entry.title: feat(anki): parse .apkg in the browser, upload only missing media
entry.content:
feat(anki): parse .apkg in the browser, upload only missing media

Deck import no longer round-trips through the server. The .apkg is parsed
in a Web Worker — @zip.js/zip.js for random-access unzip (no full-file
buffering), sql.js (SQLite-in-WASM) for the collection, fzstd for the
.anki21b format, and a hand-rolled ~100-line protobuf reader for the
media manifest, mirroring the Go decoder. After parsing, one
POST /api/media/check finds which blobs the store lacks and only those
are PUT — a re-import of a known deck uploads nothing.

This retires the biggest import pain: the chunked upload + background
parse job + status polling existed solely because shipping hundreds of
MB through Cloudflare and parsing server-side outlived the proxy
timeout. That path is untouched and remains the automatic fallback for
any client-parse failure (old browser, WASM OOM, malformed archive);
localStorage "myanki:clientParse" can force either path.

Parser parity between Go and TS is pinned by committed fixtures:
tiny-legacy.apkg (.anki2 + JSON manifest) and tiny-modern.apkg
(.anki21b + zstd + protobuf manifest) with golden JSON emitted by the
Go parser (KIROKU_GEN_FIXTURES=1 regenerates). Both parsers must
reproduce the goldens byte-for-byte; the TS suite also covers manifest
decoding, proto field skipping, zstd passthrough and mime mapping.

Memory stays flat on giant decks: media blobs stream through the hasher
one at a time, and the upload pass re-reads only missing entries from
the archive instead of retaining decoded blobs.

Verified end-to-end in Chrome against the real Go backend: import of
the fixture deck used the worker path (no /api/import-anki-package
calls), landed both blobs in the content-addressed store under the
expected hashes, and a second import produced zero PUTs.

Closes #48

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Merge pull request #47 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/media-upload-verify
entry.content:
Merge pull request #47 from Harsh-Upadhayay/feat/media-upload-verify

feat(media): verify content hash on upload, stream to disk, add bulk check

entry.title: feat(media): verify content hash on upload, stream to disk, add bulk …
entry.content:
feat(media): verify content hash on upload, stream to disk, add bulk check

PUT /api/media/{hash} previously wrote whatever body arrived under whatever
hash the URL claimed, buffering the whole blob in memory — one buggy client
could poison the content-addressed store for every device. Now the body
streams through sha256 into a temp file (io.MultiWriter, never fully in
memory), is rejected on digest mismatch or oversize (413), and lands via
atomic same-directory rename. Re-uploads of a stored hash short-circuit to
200 without reading the body.

Adds POST /api/media/check ({hashes} -> {missing}) so a client with
thousands of deck media files plans uploads/downloads with one request
instead of a HEAD per file.

Media routes are now method-specific ServeMux patterns (GET also serves
HEAD), replacing the hand-rolled method switch. Groundwork for client-side
.apkg parsing, where the browser produces media blobs the server has never
seen.

Closes #46

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
